subject: Would solving linear algebra on GPU (using e.g. ViennaCL) speed up large models?

messages.author: 9d7e54e3329f305f
messages.subject: Would solving linear algebra on GPU (using e.g. ViennaCL) speed up large models?
parts:
This question is more just out of curiosity than anything else:

I'm starting to play around with using OpenCL to parallelize C++ code to a GPU. I recently came across the ViennaCL library which enables parallelizing most basic linear algebra functionality.

It looks like ViennaCL interfaces quite nicely with Eigen, making it easy to copy Eigen objects directly into corresponding ViennaCL objects. And I think that ViennaCL has all the functionality that Stan uses in Eigen, from basic linear algebra to inverses, determinants, eigen values, and even the FFT module. The one exception is I'm not sure if it's a 1:1 match on cholesky decomposition, though ViennaCL does have some cholesky functionality.

So my question for those of you who know Stan's C++ backend better than me is: do you think that large, complicated models (e.g. those with millions of datapoints and tens of thousands of parameters - currently taking several hundred seconds for each NUTS step) might benefit from using something like this? Are there any obvious roadblocks that would make it infeasible?

If there's no glaring reasons to declare it a dead end, I'd like to try implementing a single function (e.g. maybe the Eigen solver of optimization/newton.hpp) in ViennaCL. Granted, a partial implementation will probably actually be significantly slower due to overhead in copying objects back and forth, but it should make for a proof of concept.

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Would solving linear algebra on GPU (using e.g. ViennaCL) speed up large models?
parts: Hi Kyle,
On Tue, Mar 25, 2014 at 10:06 PM, Kyle Foreman <kylef...@gmail.com> wrote:
This question is more just out of curiosity than anything else:
...

So my question for those of you who know Stan's C++ backend better than me is: do you think that large, complicated models (e.g. those with millions of datapoints and tens of thousands of parameters - currently taking several hundred seconds for each NUTS step) might benefit from using something like this? Are there any obvious roadblocks that would make it infeasible?

YES. And yes.

Within the developers, we actually don't have too much practical experience in C++ with threading / parallelization. Especially when it comes to cross-platform threading. (We have some experience in the Java world where it's much easier to multi-thread and have it implemented cross-platform.) If there's a way to do it, we'd love to hear about it and help out.

So the biggest roadblock is auto-differentiation. (Bob, if you have a chance, can you help chime in on roadblocks here?) We currently build an expression graph to do reverse-mode auto-diff by propagating the chain rule over the expression graph. I don't know if OpenCL or ViennaCL can handle parallelization over auto-diff. This is where my knowledge falls short and hopefully Bob or Matt or someone else knows how to do this.

I'm starting to play around with using OpenCL to parallelize C++ code to a GPU. I recently came across the ViennaCL library which enables parallelizing most basic linear algebra functionality.

It looks like ViennaCL interfaces quite nicely with Eigen, making it easy to copy Eigen objects directly into corresponding ViennaCL objects. And I think that ViennaCL has all the functionality that Stan uses in Eigen, from basic linear algebra to inverses, determinants, eigen values, and even the FFT module. The one exception is I'm not sure if it's a 1:1 match on cholesky decomposition, though ViennaCL does have some cholesky functionality.

The big question mark is can ViennaCL handle auto-diff variables as the first template parameter in Eigen's matrix classes? If so, then it's possible. If not, then we're S.O.L. Something that would be useful is to know what the requirements are for ViennaCL to handle parallelization. If you could provide that to the developers, we could start thinking in that direction and pushing to how we can meet those requirements.

If there's no glaring reasons to declare it a dead end, I'd like to try implementing a single function (e.g. maybe the Eigen solver of optimization/newton.hpp) in ViennaCL. Granted, a partial implementation will probably actually be significantly slower due to overhead in copying objects back and forth, but it should make for a proof of concept.

Definitely no reason to declare it a dead end.

If you're able to demonstrate how to do this, we're more than happy to help extend Stan in that direction. Right now, the dev team has its hands full, so if you wanted help implementing it you might have to wait a bit, but giving guidance is a lot less time intensive and we're able to do that at any time.
 

Thank you for bringing this up.



Daniel

parts:
On Wednesday, March 26, 2014 12:04:43 AM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
I'm starting to play around with using OpenCL to parallelize C++ code to a GPU. I recently came across the ViennaCL library which enables parallelizing most basic linear algebra functionality.

It looks like ViennaCL interfaces quite nicely with Eigen, making it easy to copy Eigen objects directly into corresponding ViennaCL objects. And I think that ViennaCL has all the functionality that Stan uses in Eigen, from basic linear algebra to inverses, determinants, eigen values, and even the FFT module. The one exception is I'm not sure if it's a 1:1 match on cholesky decomposition, though ViennaCL does have some cholesky functionality.

The big question mark is can ViennaCL handle auto-diff variables as the first template parameter in Eigen's matrix classes? If so, then it's possible. If not, then we're S.O.L. Something that would be useful is to know what the requirements are for ViennaCL to handle parallelization. If you could provide that to the developers, we could start thinking in that direction and pushing to how we can meet those requirements.

My understanding (could be wrong) is that Eigen itself has limitations when dealing with customized scalar types. With doubles, ints, etc., Eigen can ask more of the hardware (whether CPU or GPU) in terms of alignment and so forth because the hardware knows the sizes of things. There is some hint of this on the help page for using CUDA with Eigen

http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox-devel/TopicCUDA.html

In any event, this question should quickly be answerable one way or another if someone has the time to do some benchmarks with Eigen's unsupported AutoDiff module

http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/unsupported/classEigen_1_1AutoDiffScalar.html

If ViennaCL can work with that, then maybe something could be done with Stan too.

Ben

> ...

> So the biggest roadblock is auto-differentiation. (Bob, if you have a chance, can you help chime in on roadblocks here?) We currently build an expression graph to do reverse-mode auto-diff by propagating the chain rule over the expression graph. I don't know if OpenCL or ViennaCL can handle parallelization over auto-diff. This is where my knowledge falls short and hopefully Bob or Matt or someone else knows how to do this.

For many of the linear algebra operations, we're pulling
out the double parts, running the linear algebra, then using
analytic forms for the derivatives. But some of them are
done by auto-diff, and those might be hard to move.

Otherwise, no, other than the huge amount of code built into
Stan that depends on Eigen.

There's also extra overhead in just pulling out the double-based
matrix from an auto-diff (parameter) matrix. It requires allocation
and iteration.

Finally, there's the statistical problems that arise with large
matrices, namely that they're usually hard to estimate.

- Bob
